1079.title: Signs of the Spirit (CCC 694–701)
1079.hook: water, anointing, fire, cloud, seal, hand, finger and dove
1079.howItsDone: In Catholic worship the Spirit's signs are used, not only described: water at baptism, chrism at baptism and confirmation, the laying on of hands at confirmation and ordination, and the Easter candle's fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Parousia: Christ reigns now, and the day is not known. Your line was he will come. Today, pictures for the unseen.

On the table: a pitcher of water. A small bottle of oil. A lit candle. A stamp and some sealing wax. A drawing of a bird. It could be a craft-store receipt. It's actually the Catechism's list for talking about someone nobody can see. The Holy Spirit has no face in the Gospels and no human body. Jesus compares the Spirit to the wind, which you hear but can't trace. So scripture keeps reaching for things you can hold, burn, pour and watch fly.
screen: `WATER, OIL, A CANDLE.` → `A SEAL, A BIRD.` → `PICTURES OF THE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Day three hundred seven met the Spirit as the Paraclete; today, the Spirit's pictures. The Catechism walks through them one by one, and several show up again in Catholic worship. Water first: Jesus speaks of being born again of water and the Holy Ghost, so baptism pours it. Then anointing with oil. Christ means anointed, and the Catechism says the Spirit is the anointing; Catholics are anointed with chrism at baptism and confirmation. Then fire, which transforms whatever it touches. At Pentecost, in the Douay-Rheims, "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire, and it sat upon every one of them." Then cloud and light: the cloud on Mount Sinai, the cloud at the Transfiguration, and the word overshadow from Mary's story. Then the seal, close to anointing, a mark that stays; the Catechism links it to the sacraments that can't be repeated. Then the hand. Jesus heals by laying on hands, and the apostles give the Spirit the same way; the Church keeps that gesture in its sacraments. Then the finger. Jesus says he casts out devils by the finger of God, and the Catechism remembers that the law was written on stone by God's finger, and is now written by the Spirit on human hearts. Last, the dove. After the flood, Noah's dove comes back with a fresh olive branch. At the Jordan, as Jesus comes up from the water, Matthew says he saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove. So the list runs between two pictures of one Spirit: fire that changes things, and a dove that settles and brings peace.

segments.voice: Let the list pass by slowly, water, oil, fire, cloud and light, a seal, a hand, a finger, a dove, and stay with whichever one catches: water, maybe, because you showered this morning, or a hand, because someone held yours this week. Ask what it shows about something you can't see. If you pray, ask the Spirit to come in that form today; if you don't, keep that image close.
Signs of the Spirit. Scripture's pictures for the God no one can see, still used in the sacraments. Today's word.
Your line: fire and dove. Pictures you can hold, for someone you can't. Rest well.

1080.title: People, body, temple (CCC 781–810)
1080.hook: three images for what the Church is
1080.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the Church and for their parish in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and speak of the Church as the people of God, the body of Christ and the temple of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs of the Spirit, from water to the dove. Your line was fire and dove. Today, what the Church is.

What is a church? Ask a child to draw one and you'll probably get a building: a pointed roof, a door, a cross on top. That's fair; it's what the word means on a street sign. But the Catechism doesn't draw a building first. It reaches for pictures, the way scripture does, and gathers them around three: a people, a body, and a temple. Each one shows something the others miss.
screen: `A POINTED ROOF AND A DOOR.` → `NOT A BUILDING FIRST.` → `A PEOPLE, A BODY, A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Day three hundred eighteen met the body of Christ; today it's one picture of three. People first. God chose to make human beings holy not one by one, with no link between them, but as a people. The Catechism begins that story with Israel, the people God chose and made a covenant with, and reads the Church as growing out of it. The first letter of Peter says it to scattered believers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who in time past were not a people: but are now the people of God." A people has a history, a memory, a road. The Catechism lists what marks this one: you join by faith and baptism, its law is love, its mission is to be salt and light, and its destination is the kingdom. Body. Paul writes to a quarrelsome church in Corinth: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." One thing made of very different parts; the eye can't tell the hand it has no need of it. Christ is the head, the Catechism says, and the members are joined to him and to each other; when one part suffers, all suffer. A people can drift apart. A body can't, not without bleeding. Temple. Paul again: "Know you not, that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" Here the Catechism quotes Saint Augustine, echoing the lesson on body and soul: what the soul is to the human body, the Holy Spirit is to the body of Christ, the Church. One picture alone can tilt. A people without a body becomes a crowd; a body without the Spirit, a corpse; a temple without a people, an empty building.
screen: `PEOPLE: HOLY TOGETHER, NOT ALONE.` · `BODY: ONE THING, MANY PARTS.` · `TEMPLE: WHERE THE SPIRIT LIVES.` · `EACH PICTURE NEEDS THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOW THE PEOPLE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: If you belong to a parish, see it from the back pew: the regulars, the family who's always late, the person at the door, the priest; if not, take the church nearest you and the people who walk into it on Sunday. Let them be a people, a body, a house with someone home. If you pray, pray for them by name or by face; if you don't, wish them well, one by one.
People. The first of the Catechism's three pictures of the Church: God's people, made holy together. Today's word.
Your line: three pictures. A people, a body, a temple, each needing the others. See you tomorrow.

1081.title: Clergy, laity, religious (CCC 871–945)
1081.hook: different callings in one people, equal in dignity
1081.howItsDone: In Catholic parishes lay people serve as readers, catechists, musicians and parish council members, and Catholic teaching sees their everyday work and family life as their particular share in the Church's mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Church as people, body and temple. Your line was three pictures. Today, who's who in that body.

Tuesday morning at a parish. A retired nurse unlocks the food pantry and starts sorting cans. Down the hall, a sister in a plain habit runs a Bible study for new mothers. The pastor is in the office, on the phone with a family planning a funeral. A teenager is setting up chairs for confirmation class. A man who'll never set foot in the office is, at that moment, telling the truth at work when it would be easier not to. Which of them is the Church? The Catechism's answer is all of them, in different callings.
screen: `A PANTRY, A STUDY, AN OFFICE.` → `A MAN AT WORK.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE CHURCH?`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins with what everyone shares. All the baptized share in Christ's work as priest, prophet and king, each in their own way. Then a strong line: among all the faithful there is a true equality of dignity and of action, because all are reborn in Christ. Paul says it about gifts, in the Douay-Rheims: "there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord." Different jobs, same Lord, same dignity. Then the callings. Clergy are those ordained, as bishops, priests and deacons, to teach, sanctify and lead in Christ's name. Religious take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in a community the Church recognizes: the sister running the Bible study. And the laity are everyone else among the faithful: all except those in holy orders and those in the religious state. A definition by what they aren't, but it doesn't stop there. The laity have their own calling, a secular one: they seek God's kingdom by engaging in ordinary affairs, family, work, politics, culture, and ordering them toward God. The nurse sorting cans and the man telling the truth at work aren't helping the Church from outside; the Catechism says some people will hear the gospel only through them. Acts has an early picture: Priscilla and Aquila, a married couple who made tents, take a gifted preacher named Apollos aside and explain the way of God to him more fully. The Catechism also quotes Pope Pius the Twelfth saying of lay believers that they are the Church. Different callings, no ranks of worth. A bishop, a sister and a bus driver stand before God with the same baptism.
screen: `ALL SHARE CHRIST'S WORK.` · `A TRUE EQUALITY OF DIGNITY.` · `CLERGY, RELIGIOUS, AND LAITY.` · `WHERE ONLY THEY CAN REACH.` · then, large: `DIVERSITIES OF MINISTRIES, BUT THE SAME LORD.`

1082.title: The forgiveness of sins (CCC 976–983)
1082.hook: the Catechism says there is no offense the Church cannot forgive
1082.howItsDone: Catholics profess the forgiveness of sins in the Creed at Mass, and seek forgiveness for sins after baptism in the sacrament of penance, confessing to a priest and receiving absolution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the laity: clergy, laypeople and religious, different callings in one people. Your line was equal dignity.

Near the end of the Apostles' Creed, after the Church and the communion of saints, comes a short line that's easy to say too fast: the forgiveness of sins. It sits right next to some very large claims, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. That placement is a clue. The Creed doesn't treat forgiveness as a footnote for bad weeks. It puts it among the things a Catholic believes about how the whole world is put right.
screen: `A SHORT LINE, SAID FAST.` → `NEXT TO THE RESURRECTION.` → `NOT A FOOTNOTE.`

segments.voice: Back on day three, this path stepped into the confessional. Today, the line in the Creed behind it. On Easter evening, in John's Gospel, the disciples sit behind locked doors. Jesus stands among them, breathes on them, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." The Catechism ties the Creed's line to that room: forgiveness belongs with the Spirit given to the apostles, and with the Church sent out with the power to forgive. Then the doorway. The Catechism calls baptism the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness. In baptism, Catholics believe, sins are washed away completely, and a person starts clean. Then the second chance. Baptism doesn't take away human weakness, the Catechism admits, and the clean start doesn't stay clean. So for sins after baptism it turns to the sacrament of penance, confession. In its later section on confession, it borrows an old picture from early Church writers: after a shipwreck, a plank to hold on to. Then the claim itself. There is no offense, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive. No one, however wicked, should doubt that forgiveness is possible, as long as they are truly sorry. This isn't a promise that sin doesn't count. It's a promise that sorrow is never too late. The Catechism adds that Christ wants the door of forgiveness always open to anyone who turns back. So the line in the Creed is less about bookkeeping than about hope: a life can be reopened.
screen: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.` · `BAPTISM, THE FIRST FORGIVENESS.` · `A PLANK AFTER THE SHIPWRECK.` · `NO OFFENSE TOO SERIOUS.`

1083.title: The particular judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
1083.hook: at death each person meets Christ
1083.howItsDone: Catholics pray for a holy death and for the dead, and some end the day with an examination of conscience, looking back over the day before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgiveness of sins: given in baptism, offered again in confession. Your line was no sin too big.

Three crosses on a hill outside Jerusalem. On one side of Jesus, a criminal mocks him. On the other, a second criminal tells the first to stop: we deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he asks one thing: remember me when you come into your kingdom. He has no time left to make amends, no time to prove he's changed. And the answer he gets doesn't say later, or someday. It says today. That one word is where the Catechism starts on what happens at the moment of death.

This path heard the short version on day three hundred twenty-five: each person is judged by love. From the cross, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." The Catechism points to that line, and to Jesus's story of the rich man and Lazarus, to teach what Catholics call the particular judgment. Particular, because it's personal: one person, one life, at the moment it ends. First, the meeting. The Letter to the Hebrews says it plainly: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." At death, the Catechism teaches, each person meets Christ, and their whole life is seen in his light. Second, what comes next. The Catechism names three ways: into heaven at once; into heaven through a purification first, which Catholics call purgatory; or, for someone who has finally refused God's love, lasting separation from him. It doesn't say who goes where. Third, the measure. The Catechism borrows a line from Saint John of the Cross: in the evening of life, we will be judged on love. Not on titles, not on how impressive a life looked. Fourth, the hope. Saint Paul wrote that now we see only dimly, as in a dark mirror, "but then face to face." Judgment, for Catholics, isn't a file read out by a stranger. It's meeting someone, and seeing yourself the way he sees you. The thief on the cross had no record to show. He had one honest request, and a face turned toward Christ.
screen: `THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME.` · `ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER THIS.` · `JUDGED ON LOVE.` · `THEN FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Some Catholics end the day with a short look back called an examen; this is a small version. Walk back through today slowly, like watching a film, and ask where there was love, given, received or missed. If you pray, imagine looking at the day alongside Christ; if you don't, look at it the way the kindest person you know would.
The particular judgment. Catholics believe that at death each person meets Christ, and their life is seen in his light, judged, as John of the Cross put it, on love. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Not a stranger with a file, but a meeting. See you tomorrow.

1084.title: The last judgment (CCC 1038–1041)
1084.hook: all will be made plain, and God's justice and mercy seen
1084.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed at Mass that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and Matthew's scene of the sheep and the goats is among the Gospels read at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the particular judgment: each person, at death, meeting Christ. Your line was face to face.

"Lord, when did we see thee hungry?" That's the question at the center of a story Jesus tells near the end of Matthew's Gospel, just before the account of his Passion begins. A king sits on his throne with all the nations gathered before him, and he separates them, the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And here's the strange part: both groups ask the same question. The praised and the sent away are equally surprised. Yesterday was one person meeting Christ alone. Today is the whole human story, all at once, out in the open.
screen: `WHEN DID WE SEE THEE HUNGRY?` → `SHEEP AND GOATS.` → `EVERYONE IS SURPRISED.`

segments.voice: Here's the king's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Christ was there all along, in the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the prisoner, and the people who fed them didn't know it. First, the Catechism says, the last judgment shows what was really going on the whole time. Second, it's public. At the end of time, after the resurrection of the dead, every person will stand before Christ, and the truth of each life, and its relationship with God, will be laid bare. Jesus says it in Luke: "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed: nor hid, that shall not be known." Third, it's the whole story, not just one life. On that day, the Catechism says, people will see the meaning of all of history, and how God's providence led everything toward its end. It will show that God's justice wins over every injustice his creatures have done, and that his love is stronger than death. Every hidden wrong, every victim nobody listened to, finally seen. Fourth, what it asks for now. The Catechism reads this teaching as a call to turn toward God while there is time, and quotes Saint Paul: "Behold, now is the acceptable time." In the Catholic reading, the scene isn't given to frighten people about the end. It's given so they live today as if everything will one day be seen.
screen: `YOU DID IT TO ME.` · `NOTHING COVERED THAT SHALL NOT BE REVEALED.` · `JUSTICE AND LOVE, SEEN.` · `NOW IS THE ACCEPTABLE TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one part of your life you'd rather nobody looked at closely: a habit, a way you talk about someone, a small shortcut. Ask one plain question: if this were made plain tomorrow, would I change it? If you pray, ask for the courage to live in the open; if you don't, just let the question sit with you.
The last judgment. Catholics believe that at the end of time, Christ will judge all people, and everything hidden will be made plain, showing God's justice and his mercy. Today's word.
Your line: all made plain. The ones who fed the hungry never knew it was him. That's today, done.

1085.title: A new heaven and earth (CCC 1042–1050)
1085.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed their hope for the life of the world to come, and Catholic teaching connects that hope with caring for the earth in the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last judgment: the king, the sheep and the goats, and everything hidden brought to light. Your line was all made plain. Today closes the week.

Here's a question a child might ask at a funeral, out loud, where adults keep quiet: what happens to everything else? The trees, the ocean, the dog, the street you grew up on. All week the Catechism has been talking about people: their callings, their sins, their deaths, their judgment. But the Creed and the Bible don't stop at people. The last pages of scripture zoom out, to the sky and the ground. Today, the Catechism takes the child's question seriously.
screen: `WHAT ABOUT EVERYTHING ELSE?` → `ALL WEEK, PEOPLE.` → `THE LAST PAGES ZOOM OUT.`

segments.voice: This path first read John's vision on day six hundred thirty. Near the end of the Apocalypse, the Book of Revelation, John sees it. In the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth." And the one on the throne says: "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things. All things, new. That small difference is the heart of today. First, creation is waiting. Saint Paul writes to the Romans that "every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now," like a woman in labor, waiting to be set free. At the end of time, the Catechism teaches, the visible universe itself will be transformed, restored to what it was meant to be. Second, it's renewal, not replacement. Catholic teaching doesn't picture God throwing the old world away and starting over somewhere else. The universe, the Catechism says, is meant to share in the glory of the risen Christ. Same world, made whole. Third, the people are part of the picture: the final unity of the human race, God dwelling with people, every tear wiped away. Fourth, the surprise. Someone might reason that if God will renew everything anyway, there's no reason to look after the earth now. The Catechism says the opposite. Hope for a new earth should make care for this one stronger, not weaker, because what people build in love now is somehow not lost. Looking back, the week kept getting wider: a Church of many callings, sins forgiven, a soul meeting Christ, the last judgment, and now a whole creation made new.
screen: `I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.` · `EVERY CREATURE GROANETH.` · `RENEWED, NOT REPLACED.` · `HOPE THAT CARES FOR THIS EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window, or at one living thing near you: a plant, a tree, a patch of sky. Look at it the way you'd look at something you were going to keep forever: its color, its shape, the way light hits it. If you pray, thank God for what you see; if you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there.
A new heaven and earth. Catholics believe that at the end of time God will renew the whole of creation, not throw it away, and that this hope calls for care of the earth now. Today's word.
